XIMR: Options on a fund of the largest US companies plus short-term Treasury securities combine two aims over the period from March: a buffer against a slice of stock losses and a stream of premium income. It is built for investors who want equity exposure with built-in cushioning and regular payouts.
PSFM: Options referencing the big US index fund shape a defined outcome over the year from April, under Pacer and Swan's structured SOS options approach. The design targets a buffer against losses with capped gains, using a flexible options mix that can be adjusted as markets move during the period.
NISM: Small and midsize companies from markets outside the US, spanning developed and emerging economies, chosen by New York Life's investment managers. It fills the smaller-company corner of an international stock holding, a segment that tends to swing more than big foreign blue chips and gets less analyst attention.
MBND: Intermediate municipal bonds from across the US, selected with Nuveen's muni expertise for a State Street fund. The interest is exempt from regular federal income tax, so it serves as a core tax-free income holding, with professional credit research doing the work an index cannot.
FBUF: Large US stocks chosen with quantitative analysis, paired with a dynamic options buffer that Fidelity adjusts as conditions change. It is an equity hedged design aiming to keep a good share of stock market gains while reducing the depth of falls, for investors who want stocks with a shock absorber.
FTKI: Small US companies with call options sold against the small-cap index in a buy-write program that collects premium income. Small stocks already swing plenty, and the option income is meant to smooth that ride and add cash flow, at the cost of capping gains when small caps surge.
EEMO: Emerging market stocks chosen for momentum, meaning those with the strongest recent price trends, which currently puts Asian technology at about two thirds of the fund. It is a trend-following growth bet that rotates toward whichever developing markets are running hot, and it can cool just as fast.
XAUG: Options on a fund of the largest US companies shape an enhanced return over the year from August: gains get a boost up to a cap, with a moderate buffer against losses. It sits between plain buffer and growth funds, trading some protection for a faster start on the upside.
PINC: Securitized bonds actively picked by PGIM: mortgage-backed, asset-backed and commercial mortgage securities rather than ordinary company or government bonds. It is an income holding built on loan pools, where specialist credit work on the underlying mortgages and assets is the main way it tries to beat plain bond funds.
MLPD: Master limited partnerships and energy infrastructure companies, the pipeline and storage operators of North America, wrapped in a covered call strategy. It stacks two income sources, partnership distributions and option premiums, making it a high-income energy holding that gives up some upside when oil and gas rally.
BYRE: Real estate companies in the US and abroad, actively chosen by Principal managers across property types like housing, warehouses, retail and data centers. It is an opportunistic property holding that can hunt where managers see value rather than mirror the big real estate indexes, so its mix shifts over time.
ACQQ: Exposure to a laddered set of autocallable notes on the Nasdaq-100, structured products that pay income while the index behaves and can end early. Laddering spreads the notes across many start dates, and the tech-heavy index underneath makes this income stream livelier than broad market versions.
JPSV: Small US companies bought at value prices by JPMorgan managers, with banks the biggest slice at about 28 percent, plus industrial, consumer and property firms. It is an active small value holding where research into local lenders and overlooked businesses drives results rather than the small-cap index.
ESLG: Large US growth companies, over half in technology, picked by Eventide, a firm known for investing with a values lens on human flourishing. It plays the growth role with big innovators, and the managers' screening for companies creating genuine value sets it apart from plain growth index funds.
QETH: A single-cryptocurrency trust holding ether, the token of the Ethereum network, and valuing it daily at market prices. It gives brokerage-account access to the second-largest digital asset without a crypto wallet, and it moves exactly with ether, whose swings dwarf those of stock funds.
TKNZ: An actively managed basket of cryptocurrencies, spread across several digital assets rather than just bitcoin, run with the aim of beating a broad crypto index. It is a diversified-by-crypto-standards bet on the whole asset class, still far more volatile than any stock or bond fund.
IBMU: Municipal bonds that mature in December 2032, so the fund behaves like one tax-exempt bond with a known end date. It suits savers matching a future expense in that year, paying federal tax-free interest while its price swings shrink as 2032 gets closer.
AAAD: The safest slice of the CLO market: AAA-rated tranches of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of company loans, priced in dollars. These top tranches pay floating interest and sit first in line for repayment, making this a cautious income holding within a risky-sounding asset class.
USLN: Floating rate bank loans made to below-investment-grade companies, drawn broadly from the US leveraged loan market. The interest resets with market rates, so the fund suits income seekers who worry about rising rates, though the borrowers' weaker credit means losses when defaults pick up.
UFIV: Exclusively five-year US Treasury notes, a single point on the government yield curve in fund form. It is a building block for precise interest rate positioning: purer and simpler than broad bond funds, paying Treasury interest with moderate rate sensitivity and no corporate credit risk at all.
APRB: Options on a fund of the largest US companies create a defined outcome over the year from April, under Aptus managers' buffer design. It aims to soften losses with a built-in buffer while keeping a share of gains up to a cap, and the terms reset each April.
CPRO: Options on a small-cap index fund structured to protect against losses over the year starting each October, in exchange for a cap on gains. Small stocks fall harder than large ones in sell-offs, so pairing them with Calamos's full protection design targets a much smoother ride than small caps usually give.
TPFI: A core-plus bond portfolio of government, corporate and other debt, actively managed by a firm known for faith-based investing screens. It plays the steady income and ballast role, with the manager's values-based exclusions and active shifts across bond types setting it apart from a plain aggregate bond fund.
MMHI: High income municipal bonds managed by MacKay Shields: lower-rated and longer city, hospital and project debt paying richer tax-exempt interest. It is the aggressive end of tax-free income, suiting high-bracket investors who accept that weaker muni credits fall more when markets get nervous.
BUYB: Big US companies that have shrunk their share count for at least ten straight years through buybacks, spread across industry, finance and consumer sectors. Persistent buybacks signal cash-rich, disciplined firms, so this is a quality-tilted core holding built on a decade-long record rather than a single year's news.
DDNQ: An options structure on the Nasdaq-100 designed to gain in either direction over each quarter: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall, while buffering the first 5 percent of losses. The quarterly reset keeps windows short, and deep moves either way can still hurt.
NGHT: A rotation between bitcoin exposure, emphasized during overnight hours when the fund's research says crypto tends to move most, and US Treasury bills the rest of the time. It is a quirky, tactical way to hold bitcoin: part crypto bet, part cash-like safety, switching on a daily rhythm.
EBIZ: Companies that sell and deliver online: internet retailers, marketplaces, payment and logistics enablers riding the shift to e-commerce. It is a growth bet on digital shopping habits worldwide, concentrated in consumer and technology names, so it moves with online retail sentiment rather than stores.
APRH: Treasury bills paired with options on the big US stock index that pay a defined income stream unless the index falls through a 20 percent barrier during the year from April. It is built for income with a deep cushion, though crossing the barrier puts principal at risk.
TAX: US stocks above five billion dollars in size, run through Cambria's quantitative model with tax management built in from the start. It aims to keep more of its returns after tax by harvesting losses and minding holding periods, a twist most stock funds leave entirely to the investor.
JAPN: Japanese companies run by owner-operators: founders and managers who own big stakes in the businesses they lead. Horizon Kinetics hunts for that alignment of incentives in Japan's market, making this a focused bet that owner-run firms compound better than hired-management peers over time.
CTEC: Climate technology companies worldwide: solar and battery makers, electric vehicle suppliers, grid and efficiency businesses, mostly industrial firms. It is a growth bet on the build-out of clean technology, concentrated in smaller companies whose fortunes follow green energy spending and policy more than the broad market.
PRAB: Investment grade asset-backed securities, including harder-to-buy private issues alongside public ones, in a State Street portfolio. It earns income from pools of consumer and business loans, and the access to private asset-backed deals, usually reserved for big institutions, is what sets it apart.
MANI: Debt across the whole credit spectrum, from sturdy borrowers to speculative ones, actively managed by Man Group including through derivatives. It is a flexible income holding that leans on the managers' judgment about where in the credit world the pay is worth the risk at any given time.
CCOR: High-quality US companies with growing dividends, paired with options positions intended to hedge against market falls and add return. It is an equity hedged design aiming for a steadier path than plain stocks: the dividend growers provide the base, and the options overlay works as the shock absorber.
BMSI: A multisector bond portfolio from BNY Mellon, free to spread across government, corporate, mortgage and other debt sectors as its managers see fit. It plays the flexible core income role, shifting its mix with conditions rather than following any single bond index, though that freedom makes positioning vary over time.
CPNS: Options on the Nasdaq-100 fund structured to protect against losses over the year starting each September, in exchange for a cap on gains. It applies Calamos's defined protection design to the tech-heavy index, so it suits investors who want Nasdaq growth potential without facing its full drops.
ALIL: A focused portfolio of small US companies Argent managers judge to be high quality with durable competitive advantages, spread across technology, industry and finance. It is a selective small-cap holding that favors proven, well-run businesses over the speculative end of the small company universe.
DDTO: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from October, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
URAN: Uranium miners and nuclear industry companies: fuel producers at about half, plus the utilities and industrial firms that run and build reactors. It is a focused bet on nuclear power's comeback, and the miners make it far more volatile than a utility fund despite the shared theme.
NMBL: A flexible global mix that currently holds about 58 percent stocks and 27 percent bonds, plus commodities, across many countries including emerging markets. NovaTide managers shift the blend actively, making it a one-fund moderate portfolio whose risk level moves with their outlook rather than staying fixed.
FTBI: A fixed-recipe blend of income ETFs: buy-write and target income stock funds plus other income strategies across three asset classes, in set proportions. It is a balanced income holding for investors who want one ticker that automatically keeps an income-focused mix of stock and bond funds.
TEMR: Emerging market stocks researched company by company, with Asian technology near half the fund and banks about a fifth. It is an actively managed developing markets holding from a large research-driven shop, leaning into the region's chip and internet champions while spreading across many other countries.
PWS: A systematic strategy that shifts between US stocks and Treasury securities based on risk signals in its index, aiming to sidestep major market falls. It currently sits fully in stocks, spread across technology, energy, health care and property, but the WealthShield design can retreat to Treasuries when danger flashes.
SHUS: Large US stocks weighted by business risk rather than company size, using Syntax's stratified method to keep any one industry from dominating, plus index options for hedging. It aims for a more balanced big-stock portfolio than market-cap indexes give, with the options softening market drops.
AUMI: Gold mining companies worldwide, from the big producers to smaller explorers, in a single industry fund. Miners usually swing harder than gold itself because their profits are leveraged to the metal's price, so this is an amplified way to bet on gold rather than a calm store of value.
TWOX: An options design on large US companies that accelerates gains: returns aim to rise faster than the underlying stocks over each outcome period, up to a cap. It is an aggressive defined-window growth tool from iShares, where the amplification cuts both ways when the period ends in the red.
VBCJ: Corporate bonds maturing in 2036, in a Vanguard target maturity fund that will wind down as that year arrives. It works as a single rung for a known future goal, paying company bond interest while its sensitivity to interest rates steadily fades toward the end date.
TACN: A core portfolio of large companies in developed markets outside the US, actively managed, with banks the biggest slice at about a quarter. It is meant as the main international holding in a portfolio, spreading across Europe, Japan and peers with manager stock picking rather than an index.
MIVL: Large foreign companies bought at value prices by MFS managers, with banks about a third, plus industrial, staples and energy firms. It is a patient international value holding, favoring established overseas businesses trading below what the managers think they are worth, dividends and all.
